claim: Glucosinolates are characteristic of Brassicales.
source: Transporter specificity towards the recently evolved glucosinolates characteristic of Brassicales is shown to evolve prior to emergence of glucosinolate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about glucosinolates.

claim: Transporter specificity towards glucosinolates evolved prior to emergence of glucosinolate biosynthesis.
source: Transporter specificity towards the recently evolved glucosinolates characteristic of Brassicales is shown to evolve prior to emergence of glucosinolate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Glucosinolate transporters belong to the NRT1/PTR FAMILY (NPF).
source: Furthermore, we show that glucosinolate transporters belonging to the ubiquitous NRT1/PTR FAMILY (NPF) likely evolved from transporters of the ancestral cyanogenic glucosides found across more than 2500 species outside of the Brassicales.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic and functional data in the manuscript.

claim: Glucosinolate transporters likely evolved from transporters of ancestral cyanogenic glucosides.
source: Furthermore, we show that glucosinolate transporters belonging to the ubiquitous NRT1/PTR FAMILY (NPF) likely evolved from transporters of the ancestral cyanogenic glucosides found across more than 2500 species outside of the Brassicales.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic analysis and functional characterization of transporters from different species.

claim: Cyanogenic glucosides are found across more than 2500 species outside of the Brassicales.
source: Furthermore, we show that glucosinolate transporters belonging to the ubiquitous NRT1/PTR FAMILY (NPF) likely evolved from transporters of the ancestral cyanogenic glucosides found across more than 2500 species outside of the Brassicales.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the distribution of cyanogenic glucosides.

claim: Alterations in the electrogenicity of transporters accompanied changes in substrate specificity.
source: Biochemical characterization of orthologs along the phylogenetic lineage from cassava to A. thaliana, suggests that alterations in the electrogenicity of the transporters accompanied changes in substrate specificity.
evidence: This is a finding based on electrophysiological measurements of different transporters.

claim: Approximately 10% of coding sequences of contemporary genomes encode transport proteins.
source: Matching the vast structural diversity of metabolites, approximately 10% of coding sequences of contemporary genomes encode transport proteins with diverse substrate specificities (Saier and Ren, 2006) that enable transport of metabolites and ions into and out of cells.
evidence: This is cited from Saier and Ren, 2006.

claim: More than 200,000 metabolite structures have been tentatively identified in the plant kingdom.
source: New biosynthesis pathways continuously emerged throughout evolution, resulting in a vast diversity in metabolite chemical structures (>200.000 structures tentatively identified in the plant kingdom alone), where some are restricted to certain taxa and others are found broadly (Weng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Weng et al., 2012.

claim: The glucosinolate biosynthetic pathway diversified from the ancestral cyanogenic glucoside pathway.
source: As a model system, we used the Brassicales-specific glucosinolate defense compounds with a biosynthetic pathway that diversified from the ancestral cyanogenic glucoside pathway found in more than 2500 plant species (Sønderby et al., 2010a; Halkier and Gershenzon, 2006; Bak et al., 1998; Clausen et al., 2015; Mithen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources including Sønderby et al., 2010a; Halkier and Gershenzon, 2006; Bak et al., 1998; Clausen et al., 2015; Mithen et al., 2010.

claim: The cyanogenic glucoside pathway is found in more than 2500 plant species.
source: As a model system, we used the Brassicales-specific glucosinolate defense compounds with a biosynthetic pathway that diversified from the ancestral cyanogenic glucoside pathway found in more than 2500 plant species (Sønderby et al., 2010a; Halkier and Gershenzon, 2006; Bak et al., 1998; Clausen et al., 2015; Mithen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: The glucosinolate and cyanogenic glucoside pathways share the initial enzymatic amino acid to oxime conversion.
source: The two pathways share the initial enzymatic amino acid to oxime conversion, but produce structurally different end products (Clausen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Clausen et al., 2015.

claim: The glucosinolate pathway evolved to produce more than 130 glucosinolate structures with diverse amino acid-derived side chains.
source: Through an arms race between plants and interacting organisms (Bidart-Bouzat and Kliebenstein, 2008; Züst et al., 2012; Kliebenstein et al., 2005; de Vos et al., 2008; Sanchez-Vallet et al., 2010; Prasad et al., 2012; Newton et al., 2009; Fahey et al., 2001; Agerbirk and Olsen, 2012), the glucosinolate pathway evolved to produce >130 glucosinolate structures with diverse amino acid-derived side chains (Fahey et al., 2001; Agerbirk and Olsen, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Fahey et al., 2001; Agerbirk and Olsen, 2012.

claim: GTR1 and GTR2 are H+/glucosinolate symporters belonging to the NPF family.
source: Also, two H+/glucosinolate symporters, GTR1 and GTR2, belonging to the NPF family (Léran et al., 2014) and with broad glucosinolate specificity (i.e. no discrimination against amino acid side chain) were identified in Arabidopsis thaliana (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012) that predominantly produces aliphatic and indole glucosinolates (Mithen et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Léran et al., 2014 and Nour-Eldin et al., 2012.

claim: GTR1 and GTR2 have broad glucosinolate specificity with no discrimination against amino acid side chain.
source: Also, two H+/glucosinolate symporters, GTR1 and GTR2, belonging to the NPF family (Léran et al., 2014) and with broad glucosinolate specificity (i.e. no discrimination against amino acid side chain) were identified in Arabidopsis thaliana (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012) that predominantly produces aliphatic and indole glucosinolates (Mithen et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Nour-Eldin et al., 2012.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana predominantly produces aliphatic and indole glucosinolates.
source: Also, two H+/glucosinolate symporters, GTR1 and GTR2, belonging to the NPF family (Léran et al., 2014) and with broad glucosinolate specificity (i.e. no discrimination against amino acid side chain) were identified in Arabidopsis thaliana (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012) that predominantly produces aliphatic and indole glucosinolates (Mithen et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Mithen et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003.

claim: In planta studies suggest the existence of an additional glucosinolate transporter with narrow specificity for indole glucosinolates.
source: Furthermore, in planta studies suggest the existence of an additional glucosinolate transporter with narrow specificity for the recently evolved indole glucosinolates (Andersen et al., 2013) that are essential for innate immune responses (Sanchez-Vallet et al., 2010; Clay et al., 2009; Bednarek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Andersen et al., 2013.

claim: Indole glucosinolates are essential for innate immune responses.
source: Furthermore, in planta studies suggest the existence of an additional glucosinolate transporter with narrow specificity for the recently evolved indole glucosinolates (Andersen et al., 2013) that are essential for innate immune responses (Sanchez-Vallet et al., 2010; Clay et al., 2009; Bednarek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Sanchez-Vallet et al., 2010; Clay et al., 2009; Bednarek et al., 2009.

claim: NPF2.9 (GTR3) is the closest homolog of GTR1 and GTR2.
source: NPF2.9 (At1g18880, hereafter GTR3) - the closest homolog of GTR1 and GTR2 - transported I3M effectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GTR3 transports I3M effectively.
source: NPF2.9 (At1g18880, hereafter GTR3) - the closest homolog of GTR1 and GTR2 - transported I3M effectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 1C.

claim: I3M, but not 4MTB, induces negative currents in GTR3-expressing oocytes.
source: Two Electrode Voltage Clamp (TEVC) electrophysiology and time-course uptake assays showed that I3M, but not 4MTB, induces negative currents in GTR3-expressing oocytes (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: GTR3 can over-accumulate I3M, but not 4MTB, against a concentration gradient.
source: and that GTR3 can over-accumulate I3M, but not 4MTB, against a concentration gradient (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown by time-course uptake assays in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: GTR1 over-accumulated both 4MTB and I3M.
source: Alternatively, an un-coupled conductance may accompany 4MTB transport in GTR3 resulting in non-electrogenic transport or transport rates may be below the electrophysiological detection level. In comparison, GTR1 over-accumulated both 4MTB and I3M (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: GTR1 elicited negative currents of similar amplitude for both 4MTB and I3M.
source: and elicited negative currents of similar amplitude for both glucosinolates (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 have Km towards I3M less than 25 µM.
source: Plotting currents at −60 mV as a function of increasing I3M concentrations yielded a saturation curve best fitted by a Michaelis-Menten equation with Km towards I3M <25 uM for GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is determined from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 2E-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GTR3-mediated 4MTB uptake is strongly inhibited by 10% I3M.
source: Through competition assays we show that GTR3-mediated 4MTB uptake is strongly inhibited by 10% I3M, whereas 10-fold excess 4MTB does not affect I3M uptake (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is shown by competition assays in Figure 3A-D.

claim: 10-fold excess 4MTB does not affect GTR3-mediated I3M uptake.
source: Through competition assays we show that GTR3-mediated 4MTB uptake is strongly inhibited by 10% I3M, whereas 10-fold excess 4MTB does not affect I3M uptake (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is shown by competition assays in Figure 3A-D.

claim: GTR1 transports 4MTB and I3M to the same ratio as applied in the assay media.
source: In contrast, GTR1 transports 4MTB and I3M to the same ratio as applied in the assay media (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is shown by competition assays in Figure 3A-D.

claim: GTR3 imports nitrate into oocytes.
source: In accordance with previous characterization (Wang and Tsay, 2011), GTR3 imports nitrate into oocytes (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is cited from Wang and Tsay, 2011 and confirmed by data in Figure 3G.

claim: Nitrate at concentrations 100-fold in excess of I3M or 4MTB did not outcompete uptake of either glucosinolate by GTR3.
source: Nitrate at concentrations 100-fold in excess of I3M or 4MTB did not outcompete uptake of neither glucosinolate, indicating that the two substrates are not mutually exclusive (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is shown by competition assays in Figure 3E-G.

claim: GTR3 is an electrogenic transporter with a high apparent affinity and strong preference for indole glucosinolates.
source: In conclusion, our biochemical characterization shows that GTR3 is an electrogenic transporter with a high apparent affinity and strong preference for indole glucosinolates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiology and uptake data presented.

claim: GTR3 is strongly expressed in the plasma membrane of root phloem companion cells.
source: GTR3 is strongly expressed in the plasma membrane of root phloem companion cells (Wang and Tsay, 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Wang and Tsay, 2011.

claim: GTR3 is co-expressed with GTR1 and GTR2 at the tissue level in tissues according to publicly available translatome data.
source: and is co-expressed with GTR1 and GTR2 at the tissue level in other tissues according to publicly available translatome data (Mustroph et al., 2009) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is cited from Mustroph et al., 2009 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A. thaliana gtr3 mutants accumulate significantly lower concentrations of indole glucosinolates in roots compared to wild type.
source: A. thaliana gtr3 mutants accumulate significantly lower concentrations of indole glucosinolates in roots compared to wild type (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: The shift in indole glucosinolate accumulation in roots was increased in gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 triple knock-out.
source: This shift was increased in gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 triple knock-out (tko), but was not seen in gtr1 gtr2 double knock-out (dko) (Figure 4A–B, [Andersen et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4A-B and cited from Andersen et al., 2013.

claim: The shift in indole glucosinolate accumulation in roots was not seen in gtr1 gtr2 double knock-out.
source: This shift was increased in gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 triple knock-out (tko), but was not seen in gtr1 gtr2 double knock-out (dko) (Figure 4A–B, [Andersen et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4A-B and cited from Andersen et al., 2013.

claim: There is a trend, but no statistically significant increase in indole glucosinolates in the rosette of the gtr3 mutant when compared to wild type.
source: In the rosette, there is a trend, but no statistically significant increase in indole glucosinolates of the gtr3 mutant when compared to wild type (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: The gtr1 gtr2 dko shows a statistically significant increase in the rosette levels of indole glucosinolate.
source: The gtr1 gtr2 dko shows a statistically significant increase in the rosette levels of indole glucosinolate that is further increased to 4 fold when also knocking out GTR3 (gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 tko) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Rosette levels of indole glucosinolate are further increased to 4 fold in gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 tko compared to gtr1 gtr2 dko.
source: The gtr1 gtr2 dko shows a statistically significant increase in the rosette levels of indole glucosinolate that is further increased to 4 fold when also knocking out GTR3 (gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 tko) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by glucosinolate analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 all contribute to distributing indole glucosinolates between root and shoot.
source: This suggests that GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 all contribute to distributing indole glucosinolates between root and shoot.
evidence: This is inferred from the glucosinolate distribution data in mutants.

claim: MYB28 and MYB29 are key regulators of aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis.
source: As MYB28 and MYB29 – key regulators of aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis (Sønderby et al., 2010b) – are not necessary for expression of GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 (Müller et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from Sønderby et al., 2010b.

claim: MYB28 and MYB29 are not necessary for expression of GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3.
source: As MYB28 and MYB29 – key regulators of aliphatic glucosinolate biosynthesis (Sønderby et al., 2010b) – are not necessary for expression of GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3 (Müller et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from Müller et al., 2010.

claim: Only small amounts of indole glucosinolates are transported from rosette to root in heterografted plants with no glucosinolate biosynthesis in the root.
source: Analysis of heterografted plants with no glucosinolate biosynthesis in the root showed that only small amounts of indole glucosinolates are transported from rosette to root.
evidence: This is inferred from grafting experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When all three GTRs are expressed in the root, the root to rosette transport of indole glucosinolates is below detection levels.
source: Similarly, it was evident from the (qko/wt) heterografts that when all three GTRs are expressed in the root, the root to rosette transport is below detection levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by grafting experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: When all three GTRs are knocked out in roots, there is a dramatic increase in the rosette indole glucosinolate content.
source: However, when all three GTRs are knocked out in roots, we see a dramatic increase in the rosette indole glucosinolate content (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown by grafting experiments in Figure 4.

claim: GTR3 (along with GTR1 and GTR2) has a role in retaining indole glucosinolates in the root, presumably by importing indole glucosinolates into storage cells.
source: In combination, this suggests that GTR3 (along with GTR1 and GTR2) has a role in retaining indole glucosinolates in the root, presumably by importing indole glucosinolates into storage cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the grafting and mutant analysis data.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses revealed three well-defined AtGTR1-, AtGTR2- and AtGTR3-containing subclades with NPF sequences exclusively from glucosinolate-producing species of the Brassicaceae.
source: The phylogenetic analyses revealed three well-defined AtGTR1-, AtGTR2- and AtGTR3-containing subclades with NPF sequences exclusively from glucosinolate-producing species of the Brassicaceae (A. thaliana and B. rapa) (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A GTR-like subclade grouped basal to the three GTR1–3 subclades and contained GTR homologs from C. papaya and non-producing species.
source: Additionally, the analyses revealed a subclade, which grouped basal to the three GTR1–3 subclades. This subclade, which we name the GTR-like subclade contained GTR homologs from C. papaya, the most basal glucosinolate-producing species in Brassicales with a sequenced genome (Mithen et al., 2010; Goodstein et al., 2012), and from non-producing species (M. truncatula, G. raimondii, S. lycopersicum, M. esculenta and T. cacao).
evidence: This is shown by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: C. papaya is the most basal glucosinolate-producing species in Brassicales with a sequenced genome.
source: This subclade, which we name the GTR-like subclade contained GTR homologs from C. papaya, the most basal glucosinolate-producing species in Brassicales with a sequenced genome (Mithen et al., 2010; Goodstein et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from Mithen et al., 2010; Goodstein et al., 2012.

claim: The tested BrGTR3 ortholog (BrH02396) shows a strong preference for I3M.
source: Within the GTR1 and GTR3 subclades, we tested one of the respective orthologs from B. rapa and showed a strong preference for I3M by the tested BrGTR3 ortholog (BrH02396), whereas the tested BrGTR1 ortholog (BrF01711) transported 4MTB and I3M with similar efficiency (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The tested BrGTR1 ortholog (BrF01711) transported 4MTB and I3M with similar efficiency.
source: Within the GTR1 and GTR3 subclades, we tested one of the respective orthologs from B. rapa and showed a strong preference for I3M by the tested BrGTR3 ortholog (BrH02396), whereas the tested BrGTR1 ortholog (BrF01711) transported 4MTB and I3M with similar efficiency (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The high preference for indole glucosinolates appears typical for GTR3 orthologs within the Brassicales-specific GTR3 subclade.
source: Thus, the high preference for indole glucosinolates appears typical for GTR3 orthologs within the Brassicales-specific GTR3 subclade.
evidence: This is inferred from the characterization of BrGTR3 and AtGTR3.

claim: Oocytes expressing GTR-like transporters from C. papaya over-accumulate both 4MTB and I3M relative to the assay media concentration.
source: Oocytes expressing GTR-like transporters from C. papaya over-accumulate both 4MTB and I3M relative to the assay media concentration and we named them CARICA PAPAYA Glucosinolate Transporter LIKE-1 (CpGTRL1) and −2 (CpGTRL2), respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The ability of CpGTRL1 and −2 to transport both 4MTB and I3M is surprising as indole glucosinolates are found in A. thaliana and B. rapa, but not in C. papaya.
source: The ability of CpGTRL1 and −2 to transport both 4MTB and I3M is surprising as indole glucosinolates are found in A. thaliana and B. rapa, but not in C. papaya (Mithen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Mithen et al., 2010.

claim: CpGTRL2 from C. papaya transported 4MTB with a Km of 85 ± 12 µM at −60 mV.
source: Interestingly, CpGTRL2 from C. papaya transported 4MTB with a km of 85 ± 12 µM at −60 mV (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by kinetic analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: The high affinity of GTRs towards glucosinolates evolved before the diversification of the Brassicaceae and Caricaceae.
source: This indicates that the high affinity of GTRs towards glucosinolates evolved before the diversification of the Brassicaceae and Caricaceae.
evidence: This is inferred from the Km value of CpGTRL2.

claim: The common ancestor of the GTR transporters was originally broad-specific.
source: Moreover, the data imply that the common ancestor of the GTR transporters was originally broad-specific and that GTR3 lost the ability to over-accumulate aliphatic glucosinolates after the divergence of C. papaya and the ancestor of Arabidopsis and Brassica (~72.1 MYA, median of 8 studies [Hedges et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is inferred from the transport properties of CpGTRL1/2 and the phylogenetic relationships.

claim: GTR3 lost the ability to over-accumulate aliphatic glucosinolates after the divergence of C. papaya and the ancestor of Arabidopsis and Brassica (~72.1 MYA).
source: Moreover, the data imply that the common ancestor of the GTR transporters was originally broad-specific and that GTR3 lost the ability to over-accumulate aliphatic glucosinolates after the divergence of C. papaya and the ancestor of Arabidopsis and Brassica (~72.1 MYA, median of 8 studies [Hedges et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is inferred from the transport properties and phylogenetic relationships, with divergence time cited from Hedges et al., 2006.

claim: Preference for indole glucosinolates evolved as a subfunctionalization of ancestral, broad-specific glucosinolate transporters.
source: This suggests that preference for indole glucosinolates evolved as a subfunctionalization of ancestral, broad-specific glucosinolate transporters.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary analysis of transporter specificities.

claim: Oocytes expressing Me14G074000 from cassava over-accumulated both 4MTB and I3M relative to external media.
source: Oocytes expressing Me14G074000 from cassava over-accumulated both 4MTB and I3M relative to external media, while the expressed GTR homolog from cacao did not transport any glucosinolates (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The expressed GTR homolog from cacao did not transport any glucosinolates.
source: Oocytes expressing Me14G074000 from cassava over-accumulated both 4MTB and I3M relative to external media, while the expressed GTR homolog from cacao did not transport any glucosinolates (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: Cassava does not synthesize glucosinolates.
source: Hence, as cassava does not synthesize glucosinolates, the ability to transport glucosinolate appears to have arisen in the NPF family prior to the evolution of the glucosinolate biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The ability to transport glucosinolate appears to have arisen in the NPF family prior to the evolution of the glucosinolate biosynthetic pathway.
source: Hence, as cassava does not synthesize glucosinolates, the ability to transport glucosinolate appears to have arisen in the NPF family prior to the evolution of the glucosinolate biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Me14G074000 from cassava can transport glucosinolates.

claim: The characterization of Me14G074000 supports that glucosinolate transporters first evolved with broad specificity towards aliphatic and indole glucosinolates.
source: Furthermore, the characterization of this potentially ancestral form of the glucosinolate transporters support that they first evolved with broad specificity towards aliphatic and indole glucosinolates.
evidence: This is inferred from the transport properties of Me14G074000.

claim: Oocytes expressing Me14G074000 from cassava accumulated prunasin, but not linamarin, to levels equivalent to media.
source: In comparison, oocytes expressing Me14G074000 from cassava accumulated prunasin, but not linamarin, to levels equivalent to media (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 6A.

claim: The substrate-binding cavity of Me14G074000 can accommodate both cyanogenic glucosides and glucosinolates.
source: This indicates that the substrate-binding cavity of this NPF transporter can accommodate both cyanogenic glucosides and glucosinolates.
evidence: This is inferred from the transport data showing Me14G074000 transports both compound classes.

claim: Me14G074000 may represent a transition phase where specificity for cyanogenic glucosides is partially lost in favor of glucosinolate transport.
source: As Me14G074000 transports both compound classes, we propose that this transporter may represent a transition phase where specificity for cyanogenic glucosides is partially lost in favor of glucosinolate transport.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the dual specificity of Me14G074000.

claim: Glucosinolate transporters evolved from those of cyanogenic glucosides.
source: This suggests that glucosinolate transporters evolved from those of cyanogenic glucosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the characterization of Me14G074000 and MeCGTR1.

claim: Me15G180400 strongly over-accumulated prunasin and linamarin to more than 12 and 8 times the media level.
source: In contrast, Me15G180400 strongly over-accumulated prunasin and linamarin to more than 12 and 8 times the media level (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 6C.

claim: Uptake of both aliphatic and indole glucosinolates by Me15G180400 was negligible.
source: while uptake of both aliphatic and indole glucosinolates by this transporter was negligible (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Me15G180400 is specific towards cyanogenic glucosides.
source: Thus, Me15G180400 is specific towards cyanogenic glucosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the uptake data showing specificity for cyanogenic glucosides.

claim: Me15G180400 (MeCGTR1) represents the first identification of an importer of cyanogenic glucosides.
source: We named Me15G180400 MANIHOT ESCULENTA CYANOGENIC GLUCOSIDE TRANSPORTER-1 (MeCGTR1) and to the best of our knowledge, it represents the first identification of an importer of cyanogenic glucosides.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding.

claim: Prunasin and linamarin induce negative currents in MeCGTR1-expressing oocytes.
source: TEVC electrophysiology assays showed that prunasin and linamarin induce negative currents in MeCGTR1-expressing oocytes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 6D.

claim: MeCGTR1 transports prunasin with a Km of 80 ± 7 µM measured at a membrane potential clamped to −60 mV.
source: Kinetic analysis of MeCGTR1 showed that this protein transports prunasin and linamarin with a Km of 80 ± 7 µM and 262 ± 15 µM, respectively, measured at a membrane potential clamped to −60 mV (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is shown by kinetic analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: MeCGTR1 transports linamarin with a Km of 262 ± 15 µM measured at a membrane potential clamped to −60 mV.
source: Kinetic analysis of MeCGTR1 showed that this protein transports prunasin and linamarin with a Km of 80 ± 7 µM and 262 ± 15 µM, respectively, measured at a membrane potential clamped to −60 mV (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is shown by kinetic analysis in Figure 6F.

claim: MeCGTR1 is a high-affinity, cyanogenic glucoside-specific transporter capable of over-accumulating against a concentration gradient.
source: This indicates that MeCGTR1 is a high-affinity, cyanogenic glucoside-specific transporter and shows that it is capable of over-accumulating against a concentration gradient.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic and uptake data.

claim: The existence of MeCGTR1 supports the hypothesis that Me14G074000 represents a 'transition' transporter evolutionarily positioned between cyanogenic glucoside-specific and glucosinolate-specific transporters.
source: The existence of MeCGTR1 supports our hypothesis that the dual-specific Me14G074000 represents a 'transition' transporter evolutionarily positioned between cyanogenic glucoside-specific (MeCGTR1) and glucosinolate-specific transporters (GTR1–3 and GTRL1–2).
evidence: This is inferred from the characterization of both transporters and their phylogenetic relationships.

claim: The identification and close phylogenetic relationship of glucosinolate-specific, dual-specific and cyanogenic glucoside-specific transporters within the NPF supports that glucosinolate transporters evolved from cyanogenic glucoside NPF transporters.
source: The identification and close phylogenetic relationship of glucosinolate-specific, dual-specific and cyanogenic glucoside-specific transporters within the NPF supports that glucosinolate transporters evolved from cyanogenic glucoside NPF transporters.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic and functional characterization data.

claim: Most characterized members of the SLC15/PepT/POT/NPF family are symporters that function by an electrogenic proton-coupled transport mechanism.
source: Most characterized members of the SLC15/PepT/POT/NPF family are symporters that function by an electrogenic proton-coupled transport mechanism (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012; Parker and Newstead, 2014; Fei et al., 1999; Chen et al., 1999; Steel et al., 1997; Mackenzie et al., 1996; Fei et al., 1994; Doki et al., 2013; Solcan et al., 2012; Chiang et al., 2004)
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: AtGTR1 and −2 mediated transport of 4MTB induces negative currents as a result of net inward movement of protons during transport.
source: Previously, we showed that AtGTR1 and −2 mediated transport of 4MTB induces negative currents as a result of net inward movement of protons during transport (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Nour-Eldin et al., 2012.

claim: Negative currents are induced by both AtGTR1 and −2 when exposed to I3M.
source: In this study, we show that negative currents are also induced by both AtGTR1 and −2 when exposed to I3M (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: AtGTR1 and −2 transport 4MTB and I3M via a similar electrogenic transport mechanism.
source: This indicates that AtGTR1 and −2 transport 4MTB and I3M – two negatively charged glucosinolates with different amino acid side chains- via a similar electrogenic transport mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data.

claim: The tested GTR1 ortholog from B. rapa (BrGTR1) induced negative currents when exposed to 4MTB or I3M.
source: Similarly, the tested GTR1 ortholog from B. rapa (BrGTR1) also induced negative currents when exposed to 4MTB or I3M (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 5C.

claim: No detectable currents were induced by 4MTB in neither AtGTR3 nor BrGTR3.
source: No detectable currents were induced by 4MTB in neither AtGTR3 nor BrGTR3 (Figure 2A–B and Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 2A-B and Figure 5C.

claim: Electrogenic transport of - and the ability to upconcentrate - 4MTB is a property that distinguishes the GTR1 clade from the GTR3 clade.
source: Thus, it appears that electrogenic transport of - and the ability to upconcentrate - 4MTB is a property that distinguishes the GTR1 clade from the GTR3 clade.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology and uptake data comparing GTR1 and GTR3.

claim: Exposure to cyanogenic glucosides did not induce currents in Me14G074000.
source: Similarly, exposure to cyanogenic glucosides did not induce currents in the putative transition transporter, Me14G074000; (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 6D.

claim: MeCGTR1 induced negative currents when exposed to the non-charged prunasin and linamarin.
source: In comparison, MeCGTR1 induced negative currents when exposed to the non-charged prunasin and linamarin (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 6D.

claim: Transport of prunasin and linamarin by MeCGTR1 is coupled to a net influx of cationic species.
source: This suggests that transport of these two cyanogenic glucosides by MeCGTR1 is coupled to a net influx of cationic species and that transport of cyanogenic glucosides by MeCGTR1 and Me14G074000 appears to differ with respect to electrogenicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Transport of cyanogenic glucosides by MeCGTR1 and Me14G074000 appears to differ with respect to electrogenicity.
source: This suggests that transport of these two cyanogenic glucosides by MeCGTR1 is coupled to a net influx of cationic species and that transport of cyanogenic glucosides by MeCGTR1 and Me14G074000 appears to differ with respect to electrogenicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data.

claim: CpGTRL1 and CpGTRL2 induced currents when exposed to 4MTB or I3M.
source: From the GTR-like clade, the glucosinolate transporting CpGTRL1 and CpGTRL2 induced currents when exposed to 4MTB or I3M (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 5C.

claim: Me14G074000 from cassava did not induce detectable currents when exposed to glucosinolates.
source: whereas Me14G074000 from cassava did not induce detectable currents (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown by electrophysiology data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: CpGTRL1, CpGTRL2, and Me14G074000 were able to upconcentrate both glucosinolates against their respective concentration gradient.
source: All three transporters were able to upconcentrate both glucosinolates against their respective concentration gradient (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by uptake assays in Figure 5B.

claim: The glucosinolate transport mechanism first arose as a non-electrogenic mechanism that later evolved to become electrogenic.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the glucosinolate transport mechanism first arose as a non-electrogenic mechanism that later evolved to become electrogenic.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of electrophysiology data from different transporters.

claim: Electrogenic transport is not a prerequisite for the ability to over-accumulate glucosinolates.
source: Moreover, electrogenic transport appears not to be a prerequisite for the ability to over-accumulate glucosinolates.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Me14G074000 can over-accumulate glucosinolates without inducing detectable currents.

claim: Negative currents induced by AtGTR1 and AtGTR2 when exposed to negatively charged glucosinolates reflect a glucosinolate to proton stoichiometry of 1 ≤ 2.
source: Previously, we showed that negative currents induced by AtGTR1 and AtGTR2 when exposed to the negatively charged glucosinolates, reflect a glucosinolate to proton stoichiometry of 1 ≤ 2 (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Nour-Eldin et al., 2012.

claim: Substrate-dependent variation in transport coupling stoichiometry between substrate and protons has been shown to depend on the length of the oligo-peptide substrate for PepTSo.
source: Substrate-dependent variation in transport coupling stoichiometry between substrate and protons has been shown to depend on the length of the oligo-peptide substrate for PepTSo (Parker and Newstead, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Parker and Newstead, 2014.

claim: The non-electrogenic transport by Me14G074000 could indicate a different proton to glucosinolate stoichiometry compared to that of the A. thaliana orthologs.
source: The non-electrogenic transport by Me14G074000 could indicate a different proton to glucosinolate stoichiometry compared to that of the A. thaliana orthologs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: Changes in transporter substrate specificity for a given substrate may be accompanied by changes in transporter electrogenicity.
source: This would suggest that changes in transporter substrate specificity for a given substrate are accompanied by changes in transporter electrogenicity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in electrogenicity.

claim: Transport of glucosinolates became electrogenic after the divergence of cassava and C. papaya.
source: Nevertheless, the absence of induced currents by Me14G074000 indicates that transport of glucosinolates became electrogenic after the divergence of cassava and C. papaya.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: A duplication event introduced permissive mutations in a high affinity, electrogenic transporter of ancestral cyanogenic glucosides to generate a 'transition' transporter with broad, non-electrogenic glucosinolate specificity and non-electrogenic cyanogenic glucoside specificity.
source: By tracking the evolution of GTR transporter specificity towards glucosinolates, we propose that a duplication event introduced permissive mutations in a high affinity, electrogenic transporter of the ancestral cyanogenic glucosides (represented here by MeCGTR1) to generate a 'transition' transporter with broad, non-electrogenic glucosinolate specificity and non-electrogenic cyanogenic glucoside specificity (represented by Me14G074000) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the characterization data and shown in Figure 7.

claim: With the advent of glucosinolate biosynthesis and through further duplication and evolutionary divergence, the dual-specificity transporter lost its cyanogenic glucoside transport capacity and became a high affinity, electrogenic broad-specific glucosinolate transporter.
source: With the advent of glucosinolate biosynthesis and through further duplication and evolutionary divergence, our data suggests that the dual-specificity transporter lost its cyanogenic glucoside transport capacity and became a high affinity, electrogenic broad-specific glucosinolate transporter (represented by BrGTR1, AtGTRs, CpGTRL1 and CpGTRL2).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the characterization data.

claim: Further subfunctionalization within the GTR clade led to the evolution of the GTR3 subclade identified as transporters with preference and high affinity for indole glucosinolate.
source: Further subfunctionalization within the GTR clade led to the evolution of the GTR3 subclade identified as transporters with preference and high affinity for indole glucosinolate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the characterization of GTR3 and its orthologs.

claim: The subfunctionalization within the GTRs from broad to narrow specificity is contrary to the evolutionary dynamics proposed previously for substrate-transport evolution.
source: Thus, the subfunctionalization within the GTRs from broad to narrow specificity is contrary to the evolutionary dynamics proposed previously for substrate-transport evolution, where progenitor transporters had a narrow substrate specificity that expanded during evolution to become increasingly broad (Lionarons et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models cited from Lionarons et al., 2012.

claim: Five residues (P1-P3, P8 and P13) were conserved in all genes in the alignment and constitute the EXXE[R/K] motif that has an indispensable role in proton coupling.
source: Five residues (P1-P3, P8 and P13) were conserved in all genes in the alignment. These constitute the EXXE[R/K] motif that has an indispensable role in proton coupling (Table 1) (Solcan et al., 2012; Aduri et al., 2015; Jørgensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment and cited from Solcan et al., 2012; Aduri et al., 2015; Jørgensen et al., 2015.

claim: The proton coupling mechanism is conserved regardless of the substrate specificity of a NPF transporter.
source: This suggests that the proton coupling mechanism is conserved regardless of the substrate specificity of a NPF transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the EXXE[R/K] motif.

claim: Amino acid positions P7 and P9 are conserved respectively as asparagine and threonine across the GTR and cyanogenic glucoside transporters.
source: Amino acid positions P7 and P9 are conserved respectively as asparagine and threonine across the GTR and cyanogenic glucoside transporters, whereas they are glycine and asparagine residues in POT transporters and phenylalanine and asparagine residues in NPF6.3.
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: P7 and P9 could be involved in the interaction with the glucose moiety shared between glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides.
source: The only moiety shared between glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides is the glucose moiety. Thus, P7 and P9 could be involved in the interaction with the glucose moiety (Table 1, Figure 1 and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation pattern and structural similarity of substrates.

claim: Amino acid positions P4, P5 and P6 show a conservation pattern that is consistent with the changes in substrate specificity.
source: In contrast, amino acid positions P4, P5 and P6 (Figure 8 inserts) show a conservation pattern that is consistent with the changes in substrate specificity shown in this study.
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment and homology modeling in Figure 8.

claim: Position P4, P5 and P6 may contribute to determining the substrate specificity of glucosinolate and cyanogenic glucoside transporters.
source: This indicates that position P4, P5 and P6 may contribute to determining the substrate specificity of glucosinolate and cyanogenic glucoside transporters.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation pattern analysis.

claim: Before a substrate emerges, transporter specificity for the substrate may be present in transporters of chemically similar, more ancient substrates.
source: Towards understanding the evolutionary paths that lead to new transporter substrate specificities, we show that before a substrate emerges, transporter specificity for the substrate may be present in transporters of chemically similar, more ancient substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that Me14G074000 can transport glucosinolates despite cassava not producing them.

claim: As new substrates emerge, gene duplications allow multifunctional transporters to diversify through subfunctionalization into transporters with greater specificity for the new substrate.
source: As new substrates emerges (in this case glucosinolates), gene duplications allows such multifunctional transporters to diversify through subfunctionalization into transporters with greater specificity for the new substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis of the GTR family.

claim: The evolution of new substrate specificities in coupled secondary transporters is accompanied by changes in the electrogenic properties of the transport mechanism.
source: Moreover, from a mechanistic perspective, our data suggests that the evolution of new substrate specificities in coupled secondary transporters is accompanied by changes in the electrogenic properties of the transport mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiology data from different transporters.

claim: The identification of a cyanogenic glucoside transporter with high apparent affinity supports a prominent role for NPF transporters in specialized metabolism.
source: From an agro-biotech perspective, the identification of a cyanogenic glucoside transporter with high apparent affinity supports a prominent role for NPF transporters in specialized metabolism (Nour-Eldin et al., 2012; Nour-Eldin and Halkier, 2013)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the identification of MeCGTR1 and cited from Nour-Eldin et al., 2012; Nour-Eldin and Halkier, 2013.
